Using those measurements, the receiver calculates its distance from several satellites and combines the distances to find its position. This process, called trilateration, is the foundation of GPS navigation. It allows a smartphone to display your location on a map, a car to follow a route, and an aircraft to navigate without relying on a direct connection to a ground-based navigation station. Although GPS depends on satellites orbiting thousands of miles above Earth, the system does not take photographs of the ground or track every phone individually. Instead, satellites continuously broadcast signals containing information about their positions and the precise time each signal was transmitted. A GPS receiver uses that information to calculate where it is. What GPS satellites do GPS is a satellite-based navigation system developed by the United States. Its satellites orbit Earth and transmit radio signals that can be received by compatible devices around the world. How Does a GPS Satellite Tell Your Phone Where It Is? Each GPS satellite continuously broadcasts navigation signals. These signals contain information that allows a receiver to identify the satellite, determine when the signal was transmitted and estimate the satellite's position. The satellite's position is calculated from orbital information included in its navigation message. This information is important because satellites are constantly moving around Earth. A receiver cannot calculate its location accurately unless it knows where each satellite was when the relevant signal was transmitted. GPS, or the Global Positioning System, is a satellite-based technology that allows devices to determine their location, altitude, speed, and precise time. From smartphones and cars to navigation systems, GPS has become part of everyday life. But behind a simple location pin lies a network of satellites, ground stations, precise clocks, and complex mathematical calculations. For GPS to operate, several satellites need to be in orbit at an altitude of about 20,200 kilometers above Earth's surface. These satellites keep emitting radio waves that contain the satellite's exact location and very precise time. Every GPS satellite contains an atomic clock. Every GPS satellite must contain an atomic clock because it ensures precise timing for calculating the GPS receiver's location. Accurate timing is essential, as GPS uses timing information to determine distance. GPS is a satellite-based navigation system that allows compatible receivers to determine position, velocity and time. It operates through three main segments: space, control and user. The space segment consists of satellites orbiting Earth. They broadcast radio signals containing timing information and data about their orbits. The control segment includes ground facilities that monitor satellite performance, maintain system accuracy and update navigation information. The user segment consists of receivers, including those found in smartphones, vehicles, aircraft, ships and specialised surveying equipment. GPS satellites operate in medium Earth orbit, at an altitude of approximately 20,200 kilometres. The constellation is designed to provide global coverage, allowing receivers in most locations to detect signals from multiple satellites. How Does GPS Support Navigation Beyond Smartphones? GPS is used in many activities where position, movement or accurate timing matters. Aircraft use satellite navigation as part of broader navigation systems, subject to applicable operational requirements. Ships use it to support route planning and maritime navigation. Surveyors can use specialised GNSS equipment and correction methods to obtain much higher precision than ordinary consumer devices. Agriculture also benefits from satellite positioning. Precision farming systems can guide machinery along planned routes and support the management of field operations. Transport companies use location information to monitor vehicle movements and coordinate logistics.
